common_name: Jane Cowl Dahlia (Historic Giant Decorative Dahlia in Buff-Bronze Blend)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after last frost.

directions: Jane Cowl is one of the oldest named giant decorative dahlias still in cultivation, dating to the late 1920s and named for the Broadway stage actress of the same name. Its huge, informal decorative blooms open in a soft buff-to-bronze blend that can shift toward apricot and gold tones as flowers age and with changing light and temperature. Because the flowers are large and heavy, stake plants early and tie stems as they grow, and disbud the side buds around each terminal bloom to direct energy into fewer, larger flowers. Give plants rich, well-drained soil and consistent moisture through the growing season for the best bloom size.

common_name: Doris Day Dahlia (Bright Red Miniature Ball Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after last frost.

directions: Doris Day produces densely packed, perfectly spherical miniature ball blooms in a vivid, saturated red, a long-standing favorite on the exhibition show bench for its tight form and reliable color. The tightly quilled florets hold their shape well in heat and in the vase, making it a strong cut-flower choice as well as a show dahlia. Pinch out the central growing tip early to encourage branching, and remove the two side buds from each flowering stem to channel growth into a single, well-formed ball bloom. Stake plants as they develop to support the many flowering stems.

common_name: La Gioconda Dahlia (Classic Red Collarette Dahlia with Gold Collar)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after last frost.

directions: La Gioconda is one of the classic collarette dahlias, its single outer ring of broad, deep-red ray florets set off by a contrasting inner collar of smaller gold-yellow petals surrounding the open central disc. The bicolor collarette form is a magnet for pollinators since the center stays exposed, unlike fully double dahlia types. Plants branch readily and benefit from an early pinch to encourage more flowering stems, and deadheading spent blooms keeps the display going for weeks. Give plants full sun and steady moisture, and stake taller stems to keep the open-faced blooms from flopping in wind and rain.

common_name: Juanita Dahlia (Classic Dark Red Cactus Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after last frost.

directions: Juanita is a long-grown cactus-type dahlia with narrow, pointed, backward-curving petals in a rich, deep red that holds its color well through the heat of summer. The spiky, fully double blooms are held on sturdy stems that make them useful for cutting as well as garden display. Disbud the side buds around each terminal flower to produce larger, more fully formed blooms, and stake plants early since mature cactus-type flowers can be heavy. Consistent watering and a layer of mulch help keep root zones cool and even through the growing season.

common_name: Ferncliff Illusion Dahlia (Giant Lavender-Pink Decorative Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after last frost.

directions: Ferncliff Illusion, from the Ferncliff dahlia line, produces huge, fully double decorative blooms in soft lavender-pink shades that can show a lighter blush toward the petal tips. As a giant-flowered type it needs extra support: set a sturdy stake at planting time and tie in the main stem as it grows, and disbud the side buds near each terminal flower so the plant's energy goes into fewer, larger blooms. Rich, well-drained soil and even watering through the season help the big flowers develop their full size and form.

common_name: Rothesay Superb Dahlia (Exhibition Ball Dahlia in Bronze-Yellow)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after last frost.

directions: Rothesay Superb belongs to the Rothesay line of exhibition ball dahlias, carrying the tightly quilled, spherical flower form the class is known for, in warm bronze-yellow tones. The dense, evenly spiraled florets make it a reliable show-bench variety as well as a strong cut flower. Pinch young plants to encourage branching, and disbud the paired side buds on each flowering stem so the plant concentrates on producing well-formed, fully round blooms. Stake plants to keep the many flowering stems upright as the season progresses.

common_name: Kenora Fantasia Dahlia (Giant Decorative Dahlia in the Kenora Series)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after last frost.

directions: Kenora Fantasia is part of the Kenora series of large-flowered exhibition dahlias bred in Ontario, known for producing huge, fully double decorative blooms on strong stems. Because the flowers are so large and heavy, stake plants at planting time and tie the main stem as it grows, and disbud the side buds near each terminal flower to focus the plant's energy into fewer, larger blooms. Rich, well-drained soil, full sun, and steady watering through the season support the best bloom size and form.

common_name: Alstergruss Dahlia (Red Collarette Dahlia with White-Tipped Collar)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after last frost.

directions: Alstergruss is a German-bred collarette dahlia with a single outer ring of bright red ray florets and a contrasting inner collar of smaller petals tipped in white, framing the open central disc. The open-faced form is attractive to pollinators and holds up well through summer heat. Pinch young plants once to encourage bushier growth and more flowering stems, and deadhead regularly to keep new buds coming. Stake taller stems for support, and provide full sun with even moisture for the best bloom production.
